mainProgression.description: Powerful riff-based progression mixing major key chords with modal borrowing from E minor for a sophisticated rock sound

sectionProgressions.description: Synth-driven intro riff that the guitar doubles, anchored on E5 with accented chromatic movement
Guitar supports the vocal with sustained power chords and syncopated accents
Ascending progression building energy through borrowed chords resolving to the E5 tonic
Odd-time passage in 7/4 featuring stepwise power chord motion with the asymmetric meter creating rhythmic tension

harmonicFunction: E5 (I) - Strong tonic anchor; the song repeatedly returns to E as the harmonic center
D5 (bVII) - Borrowed from E Mixolydian/E minor, providing classic rock gravitas
A5 (IV) - Subdominant chord providing harmonic movement and sense of lift
C5 (bVI) - Borrowed chord from E minor adding dramatic color in the chorus
B5 (V) - Dominant function in the 7/4 section providing forward momentum
F#5 (II) - Stepwise movement chord used in the odd-time instrumental passage

techniques.name: Syncopated Power Chords
techniques.description: The main guitar riff requires precise syncopated power chord hits that lock with the synthesizer, demanding tight rhythmic accuracy and muting between strikes

notes: E5: 0-2-2-X-X-X (Open E string + 2nd fret A and D strings)
D5: X-5-7-X-X-X (5th fret A string + 7th fret D string)
A5: X-0-2-X-X-X (Open A string + 2nd fret D string)
C5: X-3-5-X-X-X (3rd fret A string + 5th fret D string)
Syncopated hits must align precisely with the synth pattern
Dead-string muting between power chord accents is essential
Attack must be aggressive and percussive
sequence: Strike E5 on the syncopated accent
Immediately mute strings after the hit
Move to next chord position during the muted gap
Hit the next accent precisely on the offbeat
tips: Listen to the synth line and learn to lock your attacks with it
Practice the rhythm pattern without chord changes first
Use palm muting and left-hand muting for clean dead notes between hits
Alex Lifeson uses a relatively clean tone with moderate gain for this riff
The rhythm is more important than the string volume - prioritize timing

techniques.name: Odd Time Signature Playing (7/4)
techniques.description: The middle instrumental section shifts to 7/4 time, requiring the guitarist to internalize an asymmetric rhythmic feel while maintaining musical flow

notes: 7/4 time can be felt as 4+3 or 3+4 groupings
In Tom Sawyer the 7/4 section feels like 4+3 (four beats then three)
Power chords move stepwise through the progression
The pattern must feel natural despite the odd meter
Neil Peart's drum pattern provides the rhythmic skeleton
sequence: Place chord changes on beat 1 of each measure
Feel the grouping as 4+3 with the accent on beat 1 and beat 5
Maintain consistent pick attack through the odd meter
Return to 4/4 smoothly when the section transitions
tips: Tap the 7/4 pattern with your foot before adding the guitar
Practice with a metronome set to 7/4 at slow tempo first
Listen to the drum pattern as your primary rhythmic guide
Don't think of it as missing a beat from 4/4 - feel it as its own groove
Record yourself to check if you are maintaining the meter consistently
details.progression: E5 - F#5 - A5 - B5 in 7/4 time

techniques.name: Palm Muting and Dynamics
techniques.description: Controlled palm muting throughout the song creates dynamic contrast between tight, percussive sections and open, ringing power chords

notes: Tight palm muting during verse to allow space for vocals and synth
Release palm mute for chorus sections for full chord sound
Gradual dynamic build through sections using muting as a volume control
Combine with dead-string muting for rhythmic percussive effects
sequence: Apply palm mute during quieter verse passages
Gradually release muting pressure during builds
Open up fully during chorus for maximum impact
Return to palm muting for next verse section
tips: The dynamic range between muted and open sections is crucial
Practice the transitions between muted and open playing
Use consistent palm pressure for even muting across all muted sections
Don't over-mute - some sustain should still come through

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: Iconic synth-led intro with guitar doubling the main riff. The syncopated power chord hits define the groove alongside Geddy Lee's synthesizer.
notes: Guitar enters with syncopated hits matching the synth line
Dead-string muting between accents is essential for the groove
Attack should be sharp and percussive
Listen to the synth for rhythmic cues

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: Guitar pulls back during verses, using palm-muted power chords to support Geddy Lee's vocals and give space to the synth textures
notes: Restrained palm-muted playing leaves room for vocals
Syncopated accents punctuate the vocal phrasing
Dynamic control is key - don't overpower the mix
Maintain tight rhythm with the bass and drums

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: Full-volume power chord progression building through borrowed chords for a dramatic, anthemic chorus section
notes: Open up from palm muting for full chord sustain
Ascending chord movement builds energy to the E5 resolution
The bVI (C5) adds unexpected harmonic color
Accentuate the arrival on E5 for maximum impact

sections.name: Middle Section (7/4)
sections.description: The famous instrumental middle section shifts to 7/4 time, featuring Alex Lifesonthe iconic vocal hooks complex drum pattern
notes: Count 7 beats per measure: 4+3 grouping
Stepwise power chord motion creates forward drive
Lock with Neil Peart's snare accents for timing reference
This section is the defining rhythmic challenge of the song

sections.name: Guitar Solo
sections.description: Alex Lifeson's guitar solo combining pentatonic licks with arpeggiated chordal passages, played over the verse/chorus progression
sections.progression: E5 - A5 - E5 - D5 (solo over verse changes)
notes: Combines single-note pentatonic runs with chordal stabs
Uses E minor pentatonic for a blues-rock flavor over the major key
String bending and vibrato for expressiveness
Returns to the rhythmic riff motif at the solo's conclusion

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: Return of the main riff with added intensity, building to the final synth-driven ending where the guitar sustains the final E5 chord
sections.progression: E5 - D5 - A5 - E5 (main riff reprise)
notes: Main riff returns at full intensity
Guitar and synth lock together for the final statement
Song ends on sustained synthesizer with guitar fading
Maintain energy and precision to the very end

guitar.recommended: Gibson ES-355 or Les Paul (Alex Lifeson's primary guitars during Moving Pictures era)
alternatives: Any semi-hollow or solid body with humbuckers
guitar.pickup: Humbuckers with coil-split capability for tonal versatility

effects.distortion: Moderate amp overdrive - not heavily distorted
effects.reverb: Short room reverb for spatial dimension
effects.other: Chorus pedal (Boss CE-1 or similar) for clean arpeggiated passages; delay for ambient washes in transitions

beginner.focus: Learn the basic power chord shapes and understand the song's structure in 4/4 sections
steps: Master E5, A5, D5, and C5 power chord shapes
Practice chord transitions at slow tempo in 4/4 time
Learn the main riff rhythm pattern without syncopation
Understand the song structure by listening and mapping sections
Play a simplified version of the verse and chorus progressions

intermediate.focus: Develop syncopated rhythm accuracy and tackle the 7/4 section
steps: Add syncopated accents to the main riff pattern
Practice dead-string muting between power chord hits
Learn the 7/4 section slowly, counting 4+3 groupings
Work on dynamic control between palm-muted and open sections
Play along with the recording at reduced tempo

advanced.focus: Master the complete arrangement including odd-time sections and solo
steps: Perform all sections at full tempo with precise syncopation
Learn the guitar solo with accurate bending and phrasing
Achieve dynamic mastery matching the original recording
Play the complete song from start to finish without errors

commonMistakes: Losing the syncopated rhythm and defaulting to straight quarter notes
Failing to mute strings between percussive power chord hits
Rushing or dragging during the 7/4 section due to unfamiliarity with odd time
Playing too loud during verses when the guitar should sit below the synth and vocals
Not paying attention to the dynamic arc between sections
practiceRoutine: Warm up with power chord changes at 60 BPM for 5 minutes
Practice the syncopated riff pattern with a metronome at 70 BPM for 10 minutes
Dedicate 10 minutes to the 7/4 section counting aloud while playing
Work on smooth transitions between sections (4/4 to 7/4 and back)
Play through the full song at 75% tempo focusing on dynamics
focusAreas: Dynamic contrast between muted and open playing
Dead-string muting technique for percussive rhythm
Locking with the rhythm section across time signature changes
metronomeWork: Practice main riff with metronome at 60 BPM, increase by 5 BPM increments to 88 BPM
Set metronome to 7/4 (or count 7 clicks) for the middle section
Practice transitions: 4 bars of 4/4 into 4 bars of 7/4 with a click
Use the metronome on beats 1 and 4 only to test internal timing
Play full arrangement with metronome on quarter notes at 88 BPM
